messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin is a 54-year-old civil servant who came to treatment months after leaving a violent relationship with a male partner who had repeatedly assaulted him in private, usually inside the apartment they had shared. What stayed with him most was not only being hit, but the feeling of being pinned inside someone else’s control: being blocked in doorways, ordered where to stand, watched when he tried to move away. On several occasions the assaults happened late at night after an argument, when the apartment was quiet and he realized no one else would hear him. He remembers the sharp, metallic taste that rose in his mouth during those episodes, and certain scenes return to him as still images—the angle of the hallway light, his partner’s shoulders filling the doorway, the bedroom seen in a kind of frozen frame. Yet when he tries on purpose to tell the story from beginning to end, he often says it goes blank and feels strangely out of reach, as if the memory will only come back on its own terms.

After the relationship ended, Martin expected that being away from his former partner would bring relief. Instead, situations that carried even a trace of that old helplessness began to unsettle him. At work in a government office, changes he could not control—a supervisor abruptly revising an assignment, a meeting being moved without warning, a security door locking behind him—could provoke an immediate inner jolt. Sleeping alone was also unexpectedly difficult. In hotel rooms on work travel, or even in his own apartment on nights his current partner was away, the silence and unfamiliarity made him feel exposed. Being alone with men could be particularly tense, especially if a male colleague lingered after others had left a conference room. In those moments, he did not simply feel nervous; the old scenes seemed to force their way in. A closed office door or the sensation of being by himself with another man could bring back those photographic flashes of the apartment and, with them, the taste in his mouth from the abuse.

Because of this, Martin has organized his life to avoid being alone, both with his thoughts and in actual rooms. He stays late near other people’s desks rather than working by himself, volunteers for collaborative tasks, and fills evenings with constant social contact so that there is always another voice in the background. If his partner is out, he will sit in a café until closing or call friends rather than spend time in the apartment by himself. He is aware this can look excessive, but to him it makes sense: being alone in a room or building feels too close to the conditions in which the abuse happened. In the same way, he tries to detach from the memories whenever they stir, pushing them off before they can fully form. Yet this way of coping seems to make the memories stranger rather than smaller. When he forces them away, he later finds he cannot deliberately retrieve what happened, and then a chance reminder will bring back a sharply isolated image or that vivid taste with alarming force.

Over time, that pattern has tightened. The more Martin arranges his days so he is never by himself, the less able he feels to tolerate moments he cannot control, and ordinary situations begin to carry more threat. At the office he now avoids being the last person left with a male coworker, sometimes inventing an errand to step out into the hallway or leaving work unfinished so he can follow the group out together. If travel is required, he dreads the hotel room more than the trip itself. He keeps the television on, calls people repeatedly, and sometimes sleeps little because lying alone in the dark seems to invite the return of those frozen images. The memories, arriving in flashes rather than in a narrative he can hold onto, make the triggers feel even more potent; and because those situations feel dangerous, he doubles down on staying surrounded by others and not letting himself think.

This has begun to affect both his work and his relationship. Colleagues have noticed that he is reluctant to take independent assignments, and his partner has become frustrated by how panicked Martin gets at the idea of a night alone. What finally brought him to seek help was a recent overnight work trip when he found himself sitting in a hotel lobby until nearly dawn rather than going back to his room, shaken after being briefly alone in an elevator with another man. He says he is frightened by how small his life has become and by the sense that these moments can still overtake him without warning. More than anything, he wants to be able to be by himself without feeling trapped, and to remember what happened without feeling as though the memory is controlling him.
